title: Symmetric positivity: determinant sign is insufficient
stem: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&a&a\\a&1&a\\a&a&1\end{bmatrix}$ to be positive definite, what is the range of $a$?
solution: Write $A=(1-a)I+aJ$. The constant-vector line has factor $1+2a$, and its orthogonal sum-zero plane has factor $1-a$. Decompose any vector orthogonally into these two parts; the quadratic form is the sum of each squared length times its corresponding factor. Strict positivity requires both factors positive, so $-1/2<a<1$, which is option 2. At either endpoint a nonzero direction has zero form, so endpoints are excluded. The determinant is $(1-a)^2(1+2a)$, but its positivity alone would wrongly admit $a>1$, where the two-dimensional plane has a negative factor. Option 1 permits a negative constant-line factor, option 3 unnecessarily excludes valid values above one half, and option 4 unnecessarily excludes valid negative values. This authentic question calibrates the distinction between determinant positivity and quadratic-form positivity.

title: Triangular polynomial map and determinant consequence
stem: On the real polynomial space $P_2$, let $T(f(x))=f(x)+(x+1)f\prime(x)$. Which set contains all eigenvalues of $T$?
solution: The ordered monomial basis is $1,x,x^2$. Its images are $1$, $1+2x$, and $2x+3x^2$. Therefore the coordinate matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\0&2&2\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}$. Its characteristic determinant is $(t-1)(t-2)(t-3)$, giving precisely eigenvalues one, two, and three, hence option 3. The printed question asks for eigenvalues; the further conclusion $\det T=6$ is our explicitly identified determinant consequence, not an added premise or changed question. It follows directly from triangularity and remains the same in every basis. Options 1 and 2 omit genuine roots, while option 4 replaces the actual degree-two factor three by four.
